docs.D00_previous_thesis_and_exit.md:
Title: The 2022 underwriting and why it was withdrawn
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/01/26170421/Pershing-Square-Capital-Management-L.P.-Releases-Letter-to-Investors-01-26-2022.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/04/20184527/Letter-to-Shareholders-4.20.2022.pdf
Date: 2022-04-20

The January 26, 2022 investor letter disclosed more than 3.1 million Netflix shares purchased beginning the preceding Friday. That is a pre-November-2025-split share count and is not comparable directly to today's shares. The underwriting emphasized streaming replacing linear television, subscription recurrence, content scale, pricing, margins and future free cash flow.

Short verbatim purchase-thesis extracts describe “subscription-based, highly recurring revenues,” “a truly best-in-class management team” and “pricing power derived from the enormous value it delivers to consumers compared with other alternatives.” Economies of scale were expected to spread content investment over a larger paying audience. Improving cash conversion was part of the case rather than a separate afterthought.

The April 20, 2022 exit letter confirms the entire investment was sold. The loss reduced funds' year-to-date returns by four percentage points. The letter did not say Netflix could never succeed. It explained that operating leverage makes intrinsic value particularly sensitive to subscriber-growth assumptions, and that recent disappointments plus a changed business model expanded forecast uncertainty.

Its explicit standard was: “We require a high degree of predictability in the businesses in which we invest due to the highly concentrated nature of our portfolio.” Management's plans to monetize account sharing and introduce advertising might be sensible, but Pershing could not confidently forecast their impact on future subscribers, revenue, margins or capital intensity.

The letter says it had “lost confidence in our ability to predict the company’s future prospects with a sufficient degree of certainty.” The issue was underwriting dispersion, not a claim that every original competitive advantage had vanished. It also emphasizes promptly acting on information inconsistent with an investment thesis.

Any fresh assessment must therefore reconcile two questions. Have advertising, paid sharing, content economics and cash conversion become sufficiently observable to restore forecast confidence? And does the price compensate for whatever uncertainty remains? A lower stock price alone cannot answer the first question, while subsequent business improvement alone cannot answer the second. The historical loss is relevant evidence about the required predictability standard, not an instruction either to avoid the company forever or to repeat the original position.
docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: Global subscription scale with a growing advertising layer
Source: compiled from: https://s22.q4cdn.com/959853165/files/doc_financials/2025/q4/FINAL-Q4-25-Shareholder-Letter.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528026000137/ex991_q126.htm
Date: 2026-04-16

Netflix sells access to entertainment through recurring memberships, with advertising on lower-priced plans and programming available across a global distribution system. Content includes licensed and internally commissioned productions. It is fundamentally a portfolio business: the economics depend on acquiring and retaining an audience over many titles rather than predicting one film's success.

The January 20 letter reports more than 325 million paid memberships in Q4 2025. It reports 96 billion viewing hours in H2 2025, up 2%, with branded-original viewing up 9%. Memberships and hours measure different things: more customers can coexist with modest aggregate-hours growth, and revenue can grow through pricing and plan mix without an equivalent increase in hours.

Scale potentially supports a reinforcing loop. A large audience spreads programming, technology and marketing costs; attractive programming supports retention and acquisition; distribution and recommendation capabilities help audiences discover titles. However, content investment is real and recurrent. It should not be described as a zero-maintenance royalty simply because delivery is digital.

Advertising revenue exceeded $1.5 billion in 2025, more than 2.5 times 2024, per the January letter. The April letter says the ad-supported plan represented more than 60% of Q1 sign-ups in countries with advertising. Those countries are not the entire world, and the figure is sign-ups, not the existing global subscriber mix. Netflix still expects roughly $3 billion advertising revenue in 2026.

The company reports consolidated financials rather than separate public subscription and advertising profit segments. Q1 revenue was about $12.25 billion, operating income $3.96 billion and margin 32.3%. The reported margin is evidence of scale economics, not a disclosed advertising margin.

Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters are co-CEOs. Reed Hastings intends not to stand for reelection at the June annual meeting. That is an announced future board transition, not a completed management departure as of April 20. Q1 fully diluted shares were 4.298 billion, and recent financial comparisons reflect the November 2025 ten-for-one split.

Moat durability depends on consumer relevance, pricing net of churn, content-spend efficiency and the ability to monetize attention. YouTube, social video, other streaming services, games and traditional entertainment compete for time and money. Scale is valuable but does not make those alternatives irrelevant.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Financial scale, cash conversion and a nonrecurring fee
Source: compiled from: https://s22.q4cdn.com/959853165/files/doc_financials/2023/ar/Netflix-10-K-01262024.pdf; https://s22.q4cdn.com/959853165/files/doc_financials/2025/q4/FINAL-Q4-25-Shareholder-Letter.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528026000137/ex991_q126.htm
Date: 2026-04-16

Dollar figures below are millions; 2024–25 figures follow the January 20, 2026 letter's rounded presentation. The 2023 10-K, filed January 26, 2024, supplies the older cash-flow observation. Small apparent differences in subtraction can reflect rounding. No missing figure is silently inferred from a different period.

| Metric | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q1 2026 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 33,723 | 39,001 | 45,183 | 12,250 approximately |
| Growth | 6.67% | 15.65% calculated | 15.85% calculated | 16% |
| Operating income | Not extracted | 10,418 | 13,327 | 3,960 approximately |
| Operating margin | Not extracted | 26.7% | 29.5% | 32.3% |
| Split-adjusted diluted EPS | Not extracted | 1.98 | 2.53 | 1.23 |
| Operating cash flow | 7,274.301 | 7,361 | 10,149 | 5,290 approximately |
| Property/equipment purchases | 348.552 | 440 | 688 | Not separately extracted |
| Free cash flow | 6,925.749 | 6,922 | 9,461 | 5,094 |
| Repurchases | Not extracted | 6,264 | 9,127 | 1,300 approximately |

Cash and equivalents were $9.034 billion at year-end 2025 versus $7.805 billion a year earlier. Short- plus long-term debt was $14.463 billion versus $15.583 billion. Calculated net debt using those definitions was $5.429 billion. Q1 cash was approximately $12.26 billion and gross debt $14.4 billion, substantially affected by a nonrecurring cash receipt.

The $2.8 billion Warner-related termination payment was recognized in interest and other income, boosting Q1 EPS and cash flow but not recurring operating income. FCF of $5.094 billion less that receipt is approximately $2.294 billion before tax/timing adjustments; this is an illustrative subtraction, not a company-defined adjusted FCF measure.

Content cash expenditure is primarily embedded in operating cash flow rather than the property-capex line. A small physical-capex number must not be mistaken for minimal economic reinvestment. The April letter expects annual cash content spending around 1.1 times amortization. Content cash-versus-expense timing is central to the earnings-to-FCF comparison.

Netflix repurchased 13.5 million shares for $1.3 billion during Q1, with $6.8 billion authorization remaining. Share count and per-share comparisons must use split-consistent data. No consistent ROIC series is included.
docs.D03_latest_results_and_guidance.md:
Title: April 16 results — strong operating growth, unchanged annual outlook
Source: compiled from: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528026000137/ex991_q126.htm; https://s22.q4cdn.com/959853165/files/doc_financials/2026/q1/Netflix-Inc-_Earnings-Call_2026-04-16T00_00_00_English-1.pdf
Date: 2026-04-16

Netflix reports Q1 revenue growth of 16%, or 14% currency-neutral, and operating-income growth of 18%. Revenue was approximately $12.25 billion and operating income $3.96 billion, with 32.3% operating margin. Management says revenue and operating income exceeded its guidance because subscription revenue was slightly stronger than planned.

Diluted EPS of $1.23 is not a clean recurring operating indicator. A $2.8 billion payment following termination of the Warner transaction was recognized outside operating income. It also materially lifted operating cash flow and FCF. Any forecast that simply annualizes Q1 EPS or FCF would capitalize a one-time receipt as if it repeated.

| April 16 outlook | Management forecast |
|---|---|
| Q2 revenue | $12.574 billion |
| Q2 revenue growth | Approximately 13% |
| Q2 operating margin | 32.6% |
| Q2 EPS | $0.78 |
| FY2026 revenue | $50.7–51.7 billion |
| FY2026 revenue growth | 12–14% |
| FY2026 operating margin | 31.5% |
| FY2026 FCF | Approximately $12.5 billion, including termination receipt |
| FY2026 advertising revenue | Approximately $3 billion |

The call's estimates table shows a $12.627 billion Q2 revenue consensus and $0.83 EPS consensus against $12.574 billion and $0.78 guidance. These are analyst estimates at the call date, not management promises. The full-year revenue and margin guidance is unchanged.

Netflix expects Q2 to have the year's highest year-over-year content-amortization growth. It expects cash content spending around 1.1 times annual amortization. That helps explain why the quarterly profit trajectory need not match revenue growth exactly.

Management says recent price changes “have gone well” and its internal primary quality-engagement metric reached a Q1 record. Those are management assessments rather than a disclosed universally comparable viewing-hours series. The January letter's 2% H2-hours increase remains a separate factual observation.

The April letter describes Warner as a potential accelerant only at the right price. With that transaction no longer pursued, current public guidance is an organic-growth case rather than a forecast of combined-company synergies. Hastings' announced decision not to seek board reelection adds a governance event, but the letter does not announce a co-CEO change.
docs.D04_price_and_valuation.md:
Title: April 20 price snapshot — a documented earnings dislocation
Source: compiled from: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/NFLX/history/?period1=1776384000&period2=1776816000; https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/institutional-investors-pile-netflix-even-113052422.html?fr=sycsrp_catchall; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528026000137/ex991_q126.htm; https://s22.q4cdn.com/959853165/files/doc_financials/2025/q4/FINAL-Q4-25-Shareholder-Letter.pdf
Date: 2026-04-20

The historical unadjusted April 20 close was $94.83, on 63,298,300 shares. The session opened at $97.14 and ranged from $93.54 to $97.60. April 17 closed at $97.31 on 125,958,700 shares after the earnings-related drop. The cutoff is the next trading day, not an asserted portfolio execution date.

A public April 1 market account gives a $134.12 52-week high and $75.01 low. These are explicitly April 1 observations rather than an independently recomputed April 20 rolling range. The cutoff close is 29.3% below that already-observed high, calculated. It is not approximately half that high. A larger drawdown at another date cannot be imported into this information set.

Multiplying the close by Q1 fully diluted shares of 4.298 billion gives a calculated diluted equity-value proxy of $407.58 billion. This is not exact capitalization based on cutoff basic shares. Subtracting approximate Q1 net cash/debt effects gives an EV proxy around $409.72 billion, using $14.4 billion debt less $12.26 billion cash. Both the share denominator and balance-sheet timing are approximate.

FY2025 EPS of $2.53 implies a calculated 37.5x prior-year P/E. That does not represent a forward multiple. Recent trailing EPS contains the termination-fee gain, so a lower headline trailing multiple can exaggerate the improvement in recurring earnings. The pack does not have an exact tax-adjusted recurring trailing EPS reconciliation.

FY2025 FCF of $9.461 billion divided by the equity-value proxy gives a calculated 2.3% historical yield. Management's $12.5 billion 2026 forecast includes the nonrecurring $2.8 billion payment; subtracting it mechanically gives $9.7 billion before possible tax/timing differences, or roughly 2.4% against the same proxy. That is a sensitivity, not company-defined normalized guidance.

A verified cutoff forward EPS consensus, forward P/E, EV/EBITDA, S&P 500 forward P/E and Netflix's own consistent five-to-ten-year valuation range are not available. Valuation comparisons require a dated forecast and consistent share-split treatment rather than an unverified headline ratio. The observed volume is large, but position-building feasibility still requires explicit participation limits and attention to price impact.
docs.D05_market_worries.md:
Title: April press — growth moderation, governance and the next monetization engine
Source: compiled from: https://www.reuters.com/business/netflix-shares-fall-after-downbeat-revenue-forecast-co-founder-leave-2026-04-17/; https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/netflix-stock-q1-2026-earnings-analysts-1236567345/; https://finance.yahoo.com/news/netflix-stock-slides-as-forecast-misses-co-founder-reed-hastings-announces-departure-from-board-215534384.html; https://s22.q4cdn.com/959853165/files/doc_financials/2025/q4/FINAL-Q4-25-Shareholder-Letter.pdf
Date: 2026-04-17

Reuters' Kritika Lamba, April 17, reports shares down more than 10% in early trading as investors digested “a tepid forecast” and Hastings' planned board departure. Its framing is uncertainty over the next growth driver as the company expands beyond its traditional subscription model. That is materially different from a claim that current operating income is falling.

Yahoo Finance's Brooke DiPalma, April 17, likewise reports a forecast miss and the cofounder's planned departure. Stronger-than-expected Q1 profits include the termination payment from the failed Warner transaction. Investors therefore have reason to focus on forward operating momentum rather than the unusually high net-income figure.

The Hollywood Reporter's Georg Szalai, April 17, describes an approximately 9% after-hours drop and quotes analysts reacting to unchanged annual guidance despite recent price increases and the abandonment of the Warner bid. The question is whether pricing and advertising can create enough incremental growth to sustain a premium multiple, rather than merely meet a forecast already embedded in the stock.

Engagement is another concrete concern. The January letter reports H2 2025 aggregate viewing hours up just 2%, below revenue growth. Higher pricing, mix and advertising can bridge that gap, but they do not permit unlimited growth without sustained consumer relevance. Management's record internal quality-engagement metric is a different metric and does not invalidate the public hours observation.

The structural bear mechanisms are competition for viewing time, weaker incremental content returns and AI-created entertainment expanding supply. Those are risks to test, not demonstrated Netflix displacement. YouTube and short-form content need not be perfect substitutes to affect engagement and advertising prices.

The governance concern is continuity after Hastings, not an announced replacement of the co-CEOs. The acquisition concern is also nuanced: abandoning an expensive transaction removes integration and financing risk, but leaves the standalone organic-growth case to justify the valuation.

The counterevidence is observable: 32.3% Q1 operating margin, 16% sales growth, a now-operating advertising business and much stronger annual FCF than in the 2022 thesis. The task is to determine whether these developments restore sufficient predictability, not to dismiss either the old forecasting failure or the current market's growth concerns.
docs.D06_peer_and_industry_benchmarks.md:
Title: Streaming competitors and the value of scale
Source: compiled from: https://investors.thewaltdisneycompany.com/news/news-details/2026/The-Walt-Disney-Company-Reports-First-Quarter-Earnings-for-Fiscal-2026/default.aspx; https://www.wbd.com/news/warner-bros-discovery-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528026000137/ex991_q126.htm
Date: 2026-04-16

Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery provide public benchmarks for subscription streaming, but neither is a pure comparable. Disney also owns experiences and sports operations; Warner includes studios and linear networks. Netflix's consolidated margin cannot be compared directly to either company's total corporate margin as if their economics were identical.

| Public observation | Netflix | Disney | Warner Bros. Discovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relevant release | April 16, 2026 | February 2, 2026 | February 26, 2026 |
| Period | Q1 2026 | Fiscal Q1 2026 | Q4 2025 |
| Streaming profitability | $3.96bn consolidated operating income; 32.3% margin | Entertainment SVOD OI $450m; 8.4% margin | Streaming adjusted EBITDA $393m |
| Relevant growth | Revenue +16% | SVOD revenue +11% | Streaming subscribers 131.6m, +3.5m sequentially |

Disney's SVOD operating income rose $189 million from $261 million, or 72%, and management attributed growth to subscription and advertising revenue, partly offset by programming, production and marketing costs. This demonstrates improving competitor economics, rather than an assumption that rivals will remain permanently loss-making.

Warner's total quarterly revenue was $9.5 billion, down 7% excluding currency, with total adjusted EBITDA $2.2 billion, down 20%. Streaming EBITDA fell 7% excluding currency. Those consolidated pressures include legacy businesses and should not be attributed automatically to HBO's consumer proposition.

Netflix's more than 325 million year-end memberships are much larger than Warner's 131.6 million streaming subscribers, but definitions differ. Scale can spread content expense across a larger paying audience and give greater flexibility to fund diverse programming. It does not establish that any particular title earns its cost or that competitors cannot retain valuable niches.

Advertising adds another competitive arena, including YouTube and social platforms. Netflix can combine premium long-form inventory with subscription revenue, but advertisers can choose many other sources of attention. Its prospective $3 billion ad revenue is still small relative to its subscription-funded business.

Cutoff peer forward multiples and harmonized FCF yields were not authenticated, so no false relative-value ranking is supplied. The measurable distinction is Netflix's demonstrated operating margin and cash conversion versus competitors' improving but different profit metrics. An analyst should distinguish that evidence from a prediction that all competition has ended.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: Warner transaction, standalone guidance and the April reset
Source: compiled from: https://ir.wbd.com/news-and-events/financial-news/financial-news-details/2025/Netflix-to-Acquire-Warner-Bros--Following-the-Separation-of-Discovery-Global-for-a-Total-Enterprise-Value-of-82-7-Billion--2025-ZTAU-tgN8w/default.aspx; https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/26/warner-bros-discovery-paramount-skydance-deal-superior-netflix.html; https://s22.q4cdn.com/959853165/files/doc_financials/2025/q4/FINAL-Q4-25-Shareholder-Letter.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1065280/000106528026000137/ex991_q126.htm; https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/NFLX/history/?period1=1776384000&period2=1776816000
Date: 2026-04-20

November 2025: Netflix effected a ten-for-one stock split. January and April 2026 shareholder-letter per-share comparisons are retroactively adjusted. Old 2022 share counts and prices need the same conversion before comparison.

December 5, 2025: Netflix and Warner announced a transaction for Warner's studios and streaming operations following the contemplated separation of Discovery Global. The announcement valued the target equity at approximately $72.0 billion and enterprise value at $82.7 billion. That headline value is not the value of all Warner activities remaining in every scenario.

January 20, 2026: Netflix reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $45.2 billion, 29.5% operating margin, more than $1.5 billion ad revenue and more than 325 million paid memberships. It forecast $50.7–51.7 billion revenue and 31.5% operating margin for 2026. The letter also disclosed modest 2% H2 viewing-hours growth.

February 26: CNBC reported Netflix was walking away after Warner's board deemed Paramount Skydance's revised offer superior. Paramount agreed to pay the $2.8 billion fee Warner owed Netflix. The abandoned transaction removes prospective financing/integration demands, while leaving any hoped-for combined-company strategic benefits unrealized. This is already public before the cutoff.

April 16: Netflix reported Q1 growth and unchanged annual revenue/margin targets. It recognized the termination fee outside operating income and in cash flow. It announced that Hastings would not seek board reelection at the June meeting, while the co-CEO structure remained in place.

April 17: Reuters reported shares down more than 10% early in the session on the forecast and governance news. Historical close was $97.31, on 125.96 million shares.

April 20: The next trading day closed at $94.83 on 63.30 million shares. This is the snapshot date. It is selected because the April earnings dislocation is independently dated, not because any particular investor's execution day is known.

Events beyond this date, later viewing data, later earnings and subsequent prices are not part of the information set. The appropriate live questions are standalone growth, advertising economics, content cash conversion and whether the reset price offers sufficient compensation for remaining uncertainty.
docs.D08_pershing_context.md:
Title: Public portfolio and the predictability hurdle
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/11144917/2026-Annual-Investor-Presentation.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/2022/04/20184527/Letter-to-Shareholders-4.20.2022.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/15162701/PSH-Fact-Sheet-December-2025-Website.pdf
Date: 2026-02-11

The February 11 presentation reports February 9 gross core-fund AUM of $19.748 billion and core equity of $16.077 billion. PSH comprised $17.872 billion gross AUM and $14.202 billion equity. Including Howard Hughes, reported gross assets were $30.040 billion. These are different measures; gross AUM includes debt, and Howard Hughes assets are not uncommitted fund cash.

The presentation gives Amazon at 13% and Meta at 10% of capital as of December 31, and Hertz at 2%. These are published portfolio-context weights, not prospective allocations for a new investment. Other public core names include Alphabet, Brookfield, Uber, Restaurant Brands, Universal Music, Howard Hughes and Fannie/Freddie exposure. Complete exact April weights and cash are unavailable.

December-quarter 13F information is public by this cutoff, but a complete independently reconciled line-item table has not been assembled here. US reportable holdings omit some foreign shares, preferreds, cash and derivatives. A 13F percentage would not automatically be a full PSH NAV percentage.

The February presentation restates core principles: “Simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business,” formidable barriers to entry, limited extrinsic-factor exposure, strong finances, minimal capital-markets dependence, and exceptional management/governance. It emphasizes valuation without reliance on future acquisitions or platform value. The stated discipline is particularly relevant after an abandoned large transaction.

Netflix-specific public history is the 2022 correspondence in D00. The April 2022 letter explains that concentrated ownership requires a high degree of predictability and that model changes widened the forecast range too much. It did not deny the possibility of subsequent business success. This standard should be applied to the currently visible advertising business, content spending and cash conversion, rather than inferred from any unpublished current ownership.

Permanent capital can support a long investment horizon, but it does not make uncertainty costless. Adding a consumer subscription/media business would diversify some industry exposure while adding sensitivity to household demand, entertainment competition and content investment. Those correlations should be evaluated alongside existing technology and consumer franchises.

No authenticated 2026 Netflix-specific public Ackman thesis statement before April 20 is supplied. The current decision must come from the pack's company evidence and the previously stated investment standard, not later disclosures.

drivers.driver: Scale and competitive position had become sufficiently established to restore confidence after 2022.
Content-spend discipline and stronger earnings-to-FCF conversion changed the underlying financial evidence.
Advertising broadens monetization and the lower-priced tier expands the addressable audience.
A large valuation reset overdiscounted engagement, AI-content and competitive concerns.

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: 9 documents including both 2022 letters. April 20 chosen after independently documented April 17 drop; exact entry day remains unpinned, so this is an early-dislocation replay, not precise execution replay. At cutoff drawdown was about 29%, not half; later half-price and 21x observations deliberately excluded. Three annual revenue/CFO/FCF observations included, some 2023 profit fields missing. Forward consensus, own-history range, market benchmark and peer valuation unavailable. Size and drivers from compendium where primary extraction was incomplete, with null rather than invented quotes.

valuation.eps_path: 15% annual EPS growth driven by low-to-mid teens revenue growth and sustained 31.5% operating margins
valuation.downside_case: Multiple compression to 18x if growth stalls to single digits and margins contract

drivers.driver: A dominant, high-growth global entertainment franchise that benefits from a reinforcing loop of programming scale, technology, and global distribution.
We are acquiring the business at an attractive 19.3x NTM P/E following a 29.3% market-driven drawdown.
The company is successfully executing a pivot to an advertising-supported model to supplement its core subscription growth.
The earnings path is supported by a consistent 15% revenue growth algorithm and disciplined capital allocation, including $1.3 billion in Q1 2026 share repurchases.
The market is incorrectly pricing in governance risk following the board departure of a founder, whereas the co-CEO structure has demonstrated operational stability.

kill_criteria: Revenue growth falls below double digits for two consecutive quarters.
Operating margins collapse below 28% due to excessive content spending or failed advertising monetization.
The co-CEO structure creates clear strategic paralysis or a shift away from disciplined capital allocation.
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A permanent deceleration in subscriber growth combined with a failure to scale the advertising business to offset content costs, suggesting the core competitive advantage is eroding.
final.memo:
The Company is a dominant, high-growth global entertainment franchise that operates an unparalleled global membership model [D02]. It meets our high standards for business quality through its reinforcing loop of programming scale, proprietary technology, and global distribution, creating a durable competitive moat [D02].

The opportunity exists because the market has overreacted to the company’s governance transition following the departure of Reed Hastings from the board [D06]. We view the recent 29.3% drawdown as a temporary dislocation rather than an impairment of the business's fundamental trajectory [D05].

At a 19.3x NTM P/E, we are able to initiate a position in a compounder at an attractive valuation relative to its future earnings power [D03, D05]. We project 15% annual EPS growth sustained by continued revenue expansion and disciplined 31.5% operating margins [D04].

Our role is that of a long-term compounder investor [D06]. We expect the market to re-rate the shares as the co-CEOs demonstrate operational continuity and the advertising revenue stream scales to become a larger, more predictable contributor to the company’s margin profile [D02, D04].

While we monitor risks related to competition and the scaling of the advertising model, we believe these are mitigated by the company's strong balance sheet, with only $2.14 billion in net debt [D03, D06]. We would change our mind if revenue growth permanently decelerated below double digits [D04].

We are initiating a position with an 8% target of NAV, as the company's large market capitalization provides sufficient liquidity for us to build our stake at current levels [D05].

valuation.eps_path: 12-14% revenue growth guidance and margin resilience driving double-digit FCF growth
valuation.downside_case: Multiple contraction to 15-18x if margins erode below 30% or dominant position is impaired

drivers.driver: Netflix is a dominant, free-cash-flow-generative global streaming leader with a massive, hard-to-replicate content and technology moat [D02, D03].
The business exhibits simple, predictable, subscription-based economics with strong 32.3% operating margins and a robust self-funding capability [D02, D03].
The recent 29.3% drawdown presents a compelling entry point for a premium business that has successfully transitioned to an advertising-supported growth model [D02, D05].
Management’s disciplined capital allocation is evidenced by the $9.127 billion returned through share repurchases in 2025 and the prudent decision to walk away from an overvalued M&A deal [D03, D08].

kill_criteria: Operating margins compress below 30% due to inefficient content spend or increased competitive churn [D02, D04]
Subscriber growth turns negative on an annual basis as the advertising model fails to offset saturation [D02, D04]
Management abandons the disciplined, self-funding capital allocation policy in favor of debt-fueled M&A or excessive share dilution [D03, D04]
Engagement metrics (viewing hours) demonstrate a sustained downward trend [D06]
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A fundamental erosion of Netflix’s dominant global streaming position, a breakdown in disciplined capital allocation following the leadership transition, or a sustained inability to grow viewing hours and advertising revenue.
final.memo:
Netflix remains the dominant global streaming leader, commanding over 325 million paid memberships through its unparalleled content library and superior recommendation technology [D02]. The business is highly free-cash-flow-generative, producing $9.461 billion in FCF during 2025, which allows the company to self-fund its growth while consistently returning capital to shareholders [D03]. Its ability to maintain margins at or above 31.5% while expanding its advertising-supported model confirms our view of it as a high-quality, predictable compounder [D02, D04].

Recent market volatility, including a 29.3% drawdown from its April high, has created a significant dislocation in Netflix's valuation [D05]. The market is fixated on short-term governance concerns following the co-founder's departure and the failed attempt at a major acquisition, incorrectly viewing these as structural impairments [D04, D06, D08]. We believe the market is failing to appreciate the strength of the underlying franchise, which continues to demonstrate double-digit revenue growth and dominant market scale [D02, D03].

At a trailing P/E of 37.5x, the stock is attractively priced relative to its long-term compounding potential [D05]. With a growth algorithm driven by disciplined content spend, pricing power, and ongoing share repurchases, we model a compelling IRR of approximately 22% [D03, D04, D05]. We believe the market will eventually re-rate the business as the durability of its FCF generation becomes more evident over the next three years [D03, D04].

Our role is to lean into this high-quality compounder as the market looks past recent irrational pessimism [D06]. We will continue to monitor the company’s operating margins and engagement metrics as key indicators of continued dominance [D02, D04, D06]. Risks include a potential margin compression due to content inefficiencies or a failure of the advertising model to offset market saturation, both of which would force us to re-evaluate our position [D02, D04].

We are initiating a target position of 8% of NAV, reflecting our high conviction in Netflix’s long-term intrinsic value [D05]. This position will be built systematically to capture the current market dislocation [D05].
